items.note: Covers what turn must achieve, how each is checked and how it is built; leaves use to the README, the caller's forms to the callers' page, prompts' wording and steps to the code.

Read from the top as a builder: goals, checks, then each approach with the parts that hold it; the picture matches the decisions in steering Task #3, including the checklist's own name and version and the end-of-run naming of side effects.
Each term is defined before use; each approach gives its parts, when they act and what they do, so nothing of how a quality is held is left to guess. Fixed: hooks were named without what they stop.
Every section serves a checklist item; the history lines ('four trials of four') were cut to one ground.
Assumptions are marked; the one trial-based ground says 'seen in trials'.
Holds purpose, decisions and reasons only; no folder names or field names that change with the build. Fixed: `.turn/` and `answer` removed.
The CCS's form and the call are left to the callers' page, use to the README; the design names only what is relied on.
Goals come before checks and build; each approach opens with its point before its parts.
Every term (caller, checklist, run, round, roles, Good, More, coverage, the run's evidence) is defined before use.
Each statement is said once; principles no longer repeat what an approach section holds. Fixed: the form clause of the second principle.
One use: understanding what turn must achieve and why it is built so.
Coverage is tied to test coverage, the first user's copy to a new team member's fresh clone.
One name each. Fixed: 'the run's record' clashed with 'the records' (the JSONL); it is now 'the run's evidence', the CCS's own word.
Headings name the quality or the approach a reader looks for.
The figure shows who takes part, what passes between them and in what order, and what turn depends on; hooks are in its last note.
Five attractive qualities, each from the README's promises.
The first-round share and time and tokens, against the version in use.
Six must-be qualities, each with what the user takes for granted and, for the repository, why.
The call, the CCS, the checklist form and what a returned CCS points to, each with who relies on it and what may change. Fixed: `.turn/` as a name became what the CCS points to.
Three non-goals with reasons.
Runs in Claude Code, Python 3.9 standard library and jq, a git repository, used by Claude.
Each attractive quality with its situation and what must happen to pass.
Both measured from the same tasks on this version and the version in use.
Each must-be quality's breaking case as a test, now including a shell side effect and a checklist without its name or version.
A test per released version calling turn as its callers did.
Five principles, each with what it protects.
The figure names user, caller, roles, scripts, Claude Code and git, and what passes between them.
Every quality is named under some approach's Achieves.
Each part says when it acts, what it looks at and what it does; each hook names its event and what it stops. Fixed: the hooks were not defined.
A Must hold under each approach.
Each choice a maintainer might change gives the option weighed and its cost; the end-of-run naming of side effects is weighed against blocking.
Each principle spans more than one approach; the hooks' session rule spans every hook.
No file names, field names, values or steps; names kept are relied on as names: `turn:up`, `next`, the CCS's parts, Esc, python3, jq. Fixed: `.turn/`, `answer`.
Headings follow the template; no section is empty.
